idiom_name: buffered chan T (MPMC hand-off); sync/atomic only when channel wakeups are too expensive
implementation_notes: Go answers the hand-off problem with channels, so the classic CAS structure is normally replaced rather than translated: a buffered chan T is a multi-producer/multi-consumer queue whose memory-model guarantee (a send is synchronized before the corresponding receive) removes the need for a CAS loop, and the runtime's own scheduler queues are lock-free internally. sync/atomic and atomic.Pointer[T] can express a Michael-Scott queue, but the memory model page tells programmers to serialise with channels and other primitives and warns "Don't be clever"; the garbage collector reclaims only what is still reachable, which prevents use-after-free but leaves ABA and shutdown reasoning to the author. Reach for atomics only in a measured hot path that must avoid channel wakeups, and keep them behind a channel-shaped API inside one package.
pitfalls: An unbuffered channel is a rendezvous, not a queue: every send waits for a receiver, which changes the latency profile completely.
Closing a channel is a broadcast of "no more values": sending after close panics and a second close panics too, so keep close to the producer.
A full buffered channel blocks the producer; if that is unacceptable the policy must be select/default (drop) or a larger buffer - Go has no overwrite mode.
